To address this, we propose NeuroPatch, a framework that patches only a minimal subset of backdoor-related erroneous neurons without modifying the neural network itself, thereby significantly reducing intervention costs and preserving model performance. Specifically, NeuroPatch first approximates the distribution of clean samples to detect backdoor-infected inputs, then ranks neurons based on the activation deviations induced by these abnormal samples. Finally, it patches the most error-inducing neurons by attaching lightweight corrective controllers to adjust their outputs, without changing the model parameters. We evaluate NeuroPatch on 168 diffusion models across two datasets and three mainstream backdoor attacks. Extensive results demonstrate both the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach: NeuroPatch achieves, on average, up to 24 × faster repair speed compared to state-of-the-art methods, while slightly improving backdoor mitigation performance. Ablation studies further confirm that ranking neurons by their error-inducing scores is a key factor driving the effectiveness of our framework. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Mospic/NeuroPatch.

Class incremental semantic segmentation (CISS) aims to enable models to incrementally acquire new knowledge in image semantic segmentation task while alleviating catastrophic forgetting of previously learned knowledge. Due to the stability-plasticity dilemma and background semantic drift, it remains a challenging task. Existing methods often omit to distinguish feature representations of new and old classes during feature knowledge distillation, leading to suboptimal adaption of new knowledge. Furthermore, the inherent class imbalance in incremental datasets can bias the model towards new classes, resulting in serious classification confusion. To address these limitations, we propose MRKD-PBCL, a novel CISS method based on Multi-level Region-wise Knowledge Distillation and Prototype Balanced Contrastive Learning. Specifically, we propose Multi-level Region-wise Knowledge Distillation (MRKD) which strategically distills knowledge by focusing on feature regions corresponding to old classes at multiple feature levels. This constrains changes of the old-class feature distribution while maintaining plasticity for learning new classes. In addition, we design Prototype Balanced Contrastive Learning (PBCL) to mitigate the impact of class imbalance. PBCL balances the gradient contribution of negative classes in contrastive learning, encouraging the model to learn more discriminative feature representations. Experiment results on the 15–1 overlapped setting of the Pascal VOC 2012 dataset show that, compared with the state-of-the-art (SOTA) method SATS, the proposed method achieves improvements of 0.89%, 6.62%, and 2.25% in base-class, new-class, and all-class mIoU, respectively.

The study focuses on developing adaptive stabilization strategies for cascade systems that couple partial differential equations (PDEs) with ordinary differential equations (ODEs) under input saturation constraints and uncertain nonlinear actuator dynamics. Since the control input appears in the ODE subsystem affected by unknown dynamics rather than directly in the PDE subsystem, the characteristic of this cascade structure makes the control task quite difficult. For this, both infinite-dimensional and finite-dimensional backstepping techniques are utilized to develop the control schemes. In particular, we apply an infinite-dimensional backstepping transformation together with its inverse to transform the original PDE subsystem into a more manageable target model, which in turn facilitates the design of the controller. Subsequently, by introducing nonlinear D-functions, a novel nonlinear first-order filter is introduced at each stage of the design to reduce the complexity arising from recursive backstepping procedures, which can overcome the drawbacks and shortcomings of traditional filters. Furthermore, by integrating the approximation capabilities of neural networks with an auxiliary system, the effects of unknown nonlinear dynamics and input saturation constraints are effectively mitigated. In addition, a self-triggered mechanism is introduced to conserve communication resources and enhance data transmission, where the next triggering instant is computed based on the current system information. Finally, the proposed framework guarantees the boundedness of all closed-loop signals, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations conducted on a Josephson junction circuit.

Memristive neural networks (MNNs) with reaction-diffusion characteristics (RDCs) have broad applications in sentiment analysis and secure communication. As two key aspects of MNNs with RDCs, stabilization and security applications constitute significant research issues. First, a new model for MNNs with RDCs is established. Compared to the existing models of MNNs with RDCs, the proposed model continuously depends on fluxes and exhibits memory properties. Second, a secure adaptive event-triggered control scheme is designed, which demonstrates robust resilience against the influence of Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks. Third, based on the established MNN model with RDCs, a new secure image communication (SIC) scheme is proposed. This SIC scheme incorporates the CRYSTALS-Kyber post-quantum key encapsulation mechanism (KEM). Compared to the existing SIC schemes, the SIC scheme with CRYSTALS-Kyber can guarantee quantum-resistant key confidentiality and ensure the security of image transmission.

Neuromorphic event cameras exhibit superior performance in low-light environments owing to their high dynamic range and microsecond-level temporal resolution. However, the intensive background activity (BA) noise inherent in low-illumination event streams significantly compromises detection accuracy. Conventional strategies predominantly utilize a decoupled pipeline where denoising and detection are treated as independent stages, often resulting in irreversible information loss and suboptimal performance due to mismatched optimization objectives. To address these challenges, we propose an end-to-end Wavelet-Enhanced Transformer detection network (WE-DETR). The proposed framework integrates the wavelet transform directly into the feature extraction hierarchy to adaptively suppress stochastic noise and enhance multi-scale structural representations from event accumulations. This is followed by a Transformer-based detection head designed to model global spatiotemporal dependencies for precise object localization and recognition. Extensive evaluations on three benchmark datasets-DSEC, Gen1, and 1Mpx-demonstrate that WE-DETR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, hardware deployment on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX achieves real-time inference at approximately 35 FPS using TensorRT FP16, validating the framework's suitability for resource-constrained embedded platforms. Field experiments in diverse outdoor scenarios under illumination as low as 2.7 lux further confirm the robustness and practical utility of WE-DETR in extremely low-light environments.

Medical image segmentation remains clinically challenging due to limited annotated datasets, complex visual variations, and the need for robust domain adaptation. Vision Transformers excel at global context modeling through pretrained representations but lack spatial inductive biases, suffering from overfitting on small medical datasets. Existing adapter-based approaches rely on fixed attention patterns and uniform window sizes, limiting adaptability to task specific regions and multi-scale medical features. We propose ViTAdapter-CWMSDA, a parameter efficient adapter architecture that introduces Cross-Window Multi-Scale Deformable Attention (CWMSDA) to address these limitations. The core innovation combines three complementary mechanisms: content-aware deformable sampling that dynamically learns spatial locations, adaptive cross-window shifting that prevents information fragmentation at boundaries, and uncertainty weighted multi scale fusion that adaptively aggregates features based on confidence scores. The frozen ViT backbone preserves pretrained knowledge while adapter modules enable medical imaging specialization with minimal parameter overhead. Comprehensive experiments on seven datasets (ISIC-2018, ISIC-2017, ISIC-2016, PH2, Kvasir-SEG, ACDC and Synapse) demonstrate consistent improvements: ISIC-2018 achieves 82.42% IoU, ISIC-2017 reaches 81.37% IoU, ISIC-2016 attains 84.28% IoU, PH2 achieves 86.10% IoU, Kvasir-SEG attains 85.39% IoU, ACDC surpasses 93.21% DSC and Synapse achieves 83.94% DSC, validating strong robustness and cross-domain generalization. ViTAdapter-CWMSDA achieves state-of-the-art performance through thoughtfully designed adaptive mechanisms while maintaining computational efficiency, training stability, and robustness required for practical clinical deployment while maintaining frozen backbone knowledge.

Blind Super-Resolution (BSR) in planetary remote sensing constitutes a severely ill-posed inverse problem, characterized by unknown degradation patterns and the complete absence of ground-truth supervision. Existing unsupervised approaches often suffer from optimization instability and distribution shifts, relying on greedy strategies or generic priors that fail to preserve distinct morphological semantics. To address these challenges, we propose History-Augmented Contrastive Mixture of Experts (HAC-MoE), a novel unsupervised framework that decouples kernel estimation from image reconstruction without requiring externally specified degradation kernels. The framework is founded on three key innovations: (1) A Contrastive Kernel Sampling mechanism that performs history-guided candidate filtering during kernel search via a composite similarity score, thereby reducing extreme outlier kernels and improving the practical stability of kernel search and initialization for the subsequent reconstruction stage; (2) A History-Augmented Contrastive Learning strategy that leverages historical model states as self-regularizing references. We provide a simplified surrogate analysis that offers an approximate interpretation of its stabilizing role, rather than a direct global guarantee for the implemented nonlinear optimization; and (3) A Morphology-Aware Soft Mixture-of-Experts (MA-MoE) estimator that dynamically modulates spectral-spatial features to adaptively reconstruct heterogeneous local planetary textures. To facilitate rigorous evaluation, we introduce Ceres-50, a benchmark dataset encapsulating diverse geological features under realistic degradation simulations. Experiments on the Ceres-50 benchmark demonstrate that HAC-MoE achieves competitive quantitative performance under physically motivated synthetic degradations in the evaluated unsupervised blind super-resolution setting. The code is available at https://github.com/2333repeat/HAC-MoE, and the dataset is available at https://github.com/2333repeat/Ceres-50.

How can convolutional neural networks (CNNs) model long-range dependencies as efficiently as Transformers? This remains a critical challenge in computer vision, particularly in medical image segmentation where accurate delineation of anatomical structures and lesions often depends on contextual cues from distant regions. To answer this, we propose omni-region convolution (ORConv), a highly efficient and effective operator that introduces surrounding contextual information into the convolution process through dynamic region partitioning and shared parameter aggregation, enabling efficient long-range dependency modeling while retaining the simplicity and efficiency of standard convolutions. Compared to window-based multi-head self-attention, ORConv achieves faster forward and backward inference while reducing memory consumption by an average of 68.1%. Building on ORConv, we further develop ORNet, a compact encoder–decoder segmentation network that integrates omni-region modeling throughout the pipeline, delivering strong accuracy while remaining lightweight and efficient. Extensive experiments on diverse medical segmentation benchmarks demonstrate strong generalization across datasets and modalities, consistently achieving state-of-the-art performance with an excellent accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

Although Vision Transformer (ViT) has demonstrated excellent performance in single image super-resolution (SISR) tasks, the global modeling nature of its self-attention mechanism often leads to over-smoothing of high-frequency details. Moreover, its inherent high computational complexity poses challenges in balancing model capacity and reconstruction accuracy. To address these issues, this paper proposes a Phase-Amplitude Collaboration Transformer (PACT), aiming to provide an efficient solution for SISR in resource-constrained scenarios. First, we design a Phase-Amplitude Collaboration and Modulation Block (PACMB), which enables more accurate extraction of high-frequency details through a two-stage process of phase-amplitude collaborative alignment and frequency-domain feature modulation. Second, an Efficient Adaptive Aggregation Block (EAAB) is proposed, based on a lightweight dual-branch attention mechanism, to achieve adaptive weighted aggregation of spatial and frequency domain features, thereby further enhancing feature representation capability. Finally, by integrating the high-frequency feature extraction advantage of PACMB and the dual-domain feature aggregation capability of EAAB, an efficient phase-amplitude collaboration Transformer architecture is constructed. To accommodate different resource constraints, we further design three lightweight versions (Tiny, PACT, and Large), achieving a balance between flexibility and practicality. Extensive experimental results show that all three versions of PACT achieve state-of-the-art performance on public benchmark datasets. Specifically, in the ×4 super-resolution task on the Urban100 dataset, each version achieves a PSNR gain of up to 0.43–0.45 dB compared to state-of-the-art models of similar complexity. Additionally, extended experiments applying PACT to image classification and real-world SR tasks further validate its superior performance and generalization capability.

The increasing structural heterogeneity and semantic complexity of logs from modern computing systems pose significant challenges to traditional anomaly detection, particularly in modeling intricate behavioral chains. This paper introduces LogPhi, an end-to-end framework for log anomaly detection that integrates the deep semantic understanding of Large Language Models (LLMs) within a dynamic knowledge-enhanced architecture. LogPhi’s architecture operates through multiple synergistic stages. First, it utilizes advanced prompt engineering to perform template-free structural normalization across 15 distinct log formats, demonstrating robust generalization capabilities. Secondly, its adaptive deduplication mechanism intelligently routes logs based on resource identifiers and employs semantic normalization to effectively reduce data redundancy. Finally, the core of LogPhi is a hierarchical detection engine grounded by dynamic domain priors. By leveraging these logical anchors to calibrate the model’s decision-making, LogPhi encourages anomaly classification to be semantically consistent and logically aligned with system constraints, substantially improving both detection accuracy and model interpretability by mitigating confident misclassifications associated with LLM hallucinations. Extensive experiments on diverse industrial datasets validate LogPhi’s effectiveness, achieving an average F1-score of 0.96—an approximately 3% improvement over state-of-the-art methods. Crucially, LogPhi demonstrates high recall for critical anomalies and exhibits exceptional robustness in cross-system transfer and zero-shot detection scenarios. By enabling automated, multi-level detection without reliance on fixed log templates, LogPhi provides a scalable and robust solution for log analysis in complex, heterogeneous environments.

Knowledge tracing is a central task in personalized education, focusing on predicting students’ mastery of various skills by analyzing their historical learning data. Although existing methods have achieved notable progress, they often fail to capture the intricate structural relationships and dependencies within learning behaviors. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a self-supervised contrastive learning approach based on a multi-dimensional graph structure (MSCL). MSCL captures complex associations between exercises by constructing a student-exercise-skill heterogeneous graph integrated with a metapath-aggregation graph neural network (MAGNN). Additionally, MSCL models the impact of learning sequences on performance by constructing interaction-directed graphs and leveraging directed graph convolutional networks (DGCNs) to represent students’ dynamic learning behaviors. Through a self-supervised graph contrastive learning mechanism, MSCL enhances the quality of heterogeneous graph embeddings, captures high-order structural features, and ultimately provides performance predictions using deep neural networks. Experimental results on four benchmark datasets demonstrate that MSCL significantly outperforms existing methods, underscoring its robustness and effectiveness in the knowledge tracing task.

Classical grid-based solvers, together with many existing physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), remain constrained when tackling multidimensional, multi-scale heat-conduction settings. The main bottlenecks are well known: the curse of dimensionality, spectral bias, and unstable training dynamics. To address these issues, we develop spatiotemporal attention-convolution physics-informed neural networks (ST-AC-PINNs) for solving multidimensional heat conduction equations. Within the standard PINNs formulation, ST-AC-PINNs combine a spatiotemporal decoupling architecture with a convolutional channel-attention module to capture multiscale spatial structure, and further introduce a progress-aware dynamic weighting strategy so that training stability and physical convergence can be improved under the same physics-informed learning paradigm. Numerical experiments demonstrate that ST-AC-PINNs achieve high accuracy with stable training behaviour, and they can be effectively applied to complex, multidimensional heat-diffusion problems, albeit with increased computational cost in multidimensional settings.

Brain tumor imaging is highly challenging due to the complex, varied structure of the tumors, which hinders effective detection. Because accurate segmentation and identification are crucial for reducing mortality rates, there is a high demand for automated, efficient methods. However, traditional techniques are often impractical for clinical settings due to low computational efficiency, loss of spatial information, and poor interpretation. In order to overcome these challenges, the research proposes an effective Modified Triplet Attention Fused Hybrid Learning Enabled Explainable Convolutional Neural Network (MTA-HXCN) framework for brain tumor detection. The research combines several advanced techniques to create a more accurate, efficient, and transparent model. The hybrid learning concept at the core of the research integrates distributed and incremental learning, while a modified triplet attention (MTA) mechanism enhances feature processing, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is incorporated to increase transparency. The Modified Triplet Attention-fused Generative Adversarial Network (MTAGAN)-based segmentation method focuses on complex, cross-dimensional feature interactions, leading to more precise segmentation results, and potentially addresses limitations of standard models. Overall, the proposed MTA-HXCN framework increases interpretability, generalization, and efficiency rather than increasing overfitting issues. Experimental results show that the proposed model achieved 97.99% accuracy, 98.36% precision, 97.80% sensitivity, 98.08% F1-score, and 98.22% specificity using the BraTS2020 dataset. Additionally, the proposed model attains 97.98% accuracy, 98.54% precision, 98.12% F1-score, 98.33% specificity, and 97.70% sensitivity using the BraTS2024 dataset, when compared to traditional approaches.

Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) have demonstrated remarkable success in solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, their performance often deteriorates as system dimensionality increases, and they typically lack incorporation of physical constraints, which is crucial for practical applications. To address these challenges, a Physics-Augmented Latent Fourier Neural Operator (PAL-FNO) framework that integrates latent space learning with physics-informed constraints is proposed to enhance computational efficiency and predictive robustness. The framework employs an autoencoder (AE) to extract low-dimensional latent representations from high-dimensional inputs and outputs, enabling an FNO to be trained in this reduced space. The pre-trained AE decoder then projects the solutions back to the high-dimensional space, where physics-based loss terms derived from governing equations are enforced to ensure physical consistency. To address differentiation inaccuracies caused by decoding errors, PAL-FNO introduces two alternative strategies: (ⅰ) incorporating a smoothness module during AE training to suppress decoding noise and (ⅱ) additionally training a neural differentiator to impose physics constraints. Numerical experiments demonstrate that PAL-FNO significantly improves computational efficiency while maintaining high prediction accuracy, providing a scalable and robust framework for solving high-dimensional PDEs.

The Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have emerged as an effective approach for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), yet they often suffer from prohibitively long training times due to their reliance on gradient-based optimization. To address this limitation, a Physical-Informed Deep Kernel Method (PiDKM) is introduced, which preserves the physics-informed framework while replacing gradient-based training with an efficient gradient-free optimization strategy. In PiDKM, kernel principal component analysis (KPCA) replaces traditional neural layers to improve nonlinear feature extraction, and dense connectivity combined with feature adhesion mechanisms is incorporated to mitigate information loss in deep representations. Kernel parameters and network configurations are automatically determined through gradient-free optimization, reducing the dependence on manual hyperparameter tuning. From the perspective of innovation and contribution, PiDKM introduces a distinct physics-informed learning framework that synergistically enhances both approximation efficiency and training robustness for PDE solutions, by integrating deep kernel representations, gradient-free optimization strategies, adaptive physical constraint weighting, and dense connectivity mechanisms. The method is validated on three canonical PDEs: the diffusion-reaction equation, the wave equation, and the Poisson equation. Comparative results demonstrate that PiDKM attains superior accuracy, with absolute error upper bounds of 10~(-3), 10~(-5), and 10~(-10), respectively, outperforming conventional PINNs, which achieves errors of 10~(-4), 10~(-4), and 10~(-6). Furthermore, PiDKM exhibits remarkable computational efficiency, achieving training speeds up to 180 times faster than conventional PINNs. These findings underscore the potential of PiDKM as a robust and efficient alternative for physics-informed deep learning for solving PDEs.

The increasing volume of sequence data in genomics poses a significant challenge for genomic sequence classification in bioinformatics. As rapidly growing genomic data require more efficient and scalable strategies, an opportunity exists for Quantum Machine Learning to improve the processing of high dimensional biological data. Unfortunately, the integration of quantum machine learning into real-world genomic classification has not yet been examined. To fill this gap, we propose a hybrid quantum-classical neural network for genomic sequence classification (QNN-GSC). The QNN-GSC utilizes classical preprocessing with a quantum feature map custom designed to represent complex correlations and dependencies among the data in genomic sequences. The encoded data is then processed using a quantum neural network (QNN) architecture. Using four open-source benchmark genomic datasets allows us to empirically evaluate the performance of QNN-GSC for genomic classification. Empirical evaluation showed that QNN-GSC demonstrates better performance by achieving macro-average Area Under Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve (AUC) value of 0.757, an average F1-score of 0.711, and an average Geometric Mean (G-mean) value of 0.665. The performance of the QNN-GSC has also been statistically evaluated which further confirms its effectiveness. In addition, we also provided a quantum characterization of the proposed feature map through expressibility (D_(K L) = 0.101), entanglement capability (Q_(M W) - 0.821), and noise robustness analysis under four noise channels, which confirms that the custom feature map performs better than the standard Qiskit feature maps in entanglement while maintaining a trainability-safe expressibility level.

Hard-Constrained Physics-Informed Neural Networks (HC-PINNs) embed boundary conditions directly into the network architecture through specially designed trial functions, yet their practical performance is often bot-tlenecked by boundary function construction and hyperparameter tuning on complex geometries. This work introduces a theoretically-grounded automated design criterion based on Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) spectral analysis, connecting boundary function choices to training dynamics. The effective rank (r_(eff)) of the residual NTK matrix is identified as a training-free performance predictor, and an NTK-guided Bayesian Optimization framework is developed to efficiently tune boundary-function hyperparameters. On star-shaped and gear-shaped benchmarks, the proposed method achieves 89.2%-90.8% time reduction compared to exhaustive grid search, with identified configurations consistently outperforming 97% of grid search attempts. Overall, a systematic pathway is established from NTK theory to automated boundary function design, enabling quantitative, theory-driven HC-PINN configuration with order-of-magnitude computational savings.

Physics-informed deep operator network (DeepONet) has achieved remarkable success in solving partial differential equations (PDEs), yet its convergence is often slow. To address this issue, we have proposed a causality segmental time-domain training method to accelerate physics-informed DeepONet. The temporal horizon of the operator learning task is partitioned into multiple subintervals. To enforce causality during training, each temporal subinterval is assigned a weight that adapts to the evolution of the residual loss. This segmental weighting prioritises early segments until their residuals are sufficiently reduced, after which later segments are progressively optimised. Compared with the standard physics-informed DeepONet, the proposed method has significantly accelerated convergence and reduced prediction error. A series of numerical experiments has validated the effectiveness of the proposed training method. The causality segmental time-domain training method attains a balance between respecting temporal causality and leveraging the network's global optimisation capabilities within each segment, markedly enhancing the training efficiency and predictive accuracy of the physics-informed DeepONet.

Methods based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Transformers have achieved promising performance in medical image segmentation. However, most models use only images as input, neglecting the auxiliary role of multimodal information. A few models utilize both text and image data, but their effectiveness is often limited to specific datasets. How to fully exploit the one-dimensional sequence processing advantages of Transformers to design a multimodal segmentation paradigm for medical imaging remains an open question. In this work, we propose a multimodal segmentation paradigm called MLAT, which enables accurate medical image segmentation through simple text annotations. Specifically, for medical images with different characteristics, we automatically generate simple text descriptions containing only basic information such as position and quantity. A dual-branch architecture is used to process both text and image data. The designed Vision-Language Interaction Gate (VLIG) module enables fine-grained multimodal feature interaction, while the Adaptive Reconstruct Fusion (ARF) module dynamically fuses reconstructed and original features. We further propose a hybrid loss function to supervise the degree of text-image fusion at different hierarchical levels. Extensive experiments across ten different types of datasets demonstrate that our proposed paradigm surpasses state-of-the-art methods in segmentation accuracy, including CNN-based, Transformer-based, hybrid CNN-Transformer models, and other multimodal fusion frameworks.

Considering unknown transmission disturbances, this work explores the adaptive control design for linear parabolic partial differential equation (PDE) systems equipped with mobile sensors and actuators. First, for the case of constant transmission disturbances, a unified framework for adaptive control and guidance is formulated to ensure the asymptotic stability of the closed-loop PDE dynamics. Subsequently, a radial basis function neural network (NN) with an adaptive weight adjustment mechanism is employed to estimate unknown nonlinear transmission disturbances. Then, the adaptive neural control laws and mobile actuator/sensor guidance laws are developed to guarantee that the closed-loop PDE system is uniformly ultimately bounded. Furthermore, the designed mobile actuator/sensor guidance laws aim to enhance the transient response of closed-loop state. Finally, numerical experiments on a diffusion process validate the efficacy of the suggested methodology.

Downscaling coarse-resolution reanalysis data to high-resolution profiles is crucial for enhancing climate modeling precision. Existing methods often produce over-smoothed results, fail to capture fine-scale features, and lack robust uncertainty quantification. To this end, we introduce OceanSR-Prob, a generative diffusion-based framework for spatial downscaling of global oceanic wind speed profiles. OceanSR-Prob is designed to model the conditional distribution of high-resolution profiles, which enables ensemble sampling and uncertainty quantification. The land-sea mask is integrated into the model to ensure physical consistency. To enable efficient global downscaling, a patch-overlap strategy is employed to facilitate parallel processing, complemented by a lightweight stitching network that integrates patches and minimizes boundary artifacts. The test results on the CCMP 3.1 dataset show that OceanSR-Prob achieves satisfactory downscaling performance and outperforms baseline methods in accuracy and preservation of fine-scale details. In particular, the results of two typhoon events demonstrate OceanSR-Prob’s ability to precisely characterize the distributions of wind speed extremes and their locations, supporting robust analysis of critical climate phenomena. Alternatively, OceanSR-Deter offers a deterministic variant prioritizing inference speed over probabilistic refinement. These advances position OceanSR as a robust framework for high-resolution modeling of climate systems, with important implications for climate risk management, extreme event analysis, and renewable energy applications.

Water-surface object detection is pivotal for intelligent maritime navigation and environmental monitoring. While Artificial Neural Network (ANN)-based detectors deliver strong performance, their intensive computational and energy demands often exceed the stringent Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) constraints of unmanned surface platforms. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer an energy-efficient alternative; however, existing deep SNNs suffer from an intrinsic low-pass spectral bias driven by repeated integration-and-leak operations. This bias attenuates high-frequency discriminative cues—such as object boundaries and fine-grained textures—which are critical for distinguishing small maritime targets from dynamic water backgrounds. To bridge this gap, we propose Spiking Water-Surface YOLO (SWS-YOLO), a high-performance, energy-efficient SNN detector tailored for maritime perception. Distinct from ANN-to-SNN conversion, SWS-YOLO utilizes direct integer-valued training. To improve feature representation under dynamic water-surface conditions, two neuromorphic innovations are introduced. First, a Multi-Synaptic Firing (MSF) neuron is incorporated to boost representational capacity for inputs with varying intensities through parallel synaptic pathways and multi-level thresholds. Second, a Multi-step High-Frequency Retention Module (MHFRM) is designed to explicitly counteract the spectral attenuation of high-frequency details through temporal residual compensation across multiple time steps. Experimental results on the self-collected YZ-EXT and the public WSODD datasets demonstrate that SWS-YOLO achieves a favorable balance between detection accuracy and energy efficiency. With 12.1 M parameters, the proposed model reaches 80.6% mAP@0.5 on YZ-EXT with an energy consumption of only 40.8 mJ per inference. This result demonstrates approximately 4.4 × higher energy efficiency compared to YOLOv8m and a 4.6% performance improvement over the state-of-the-art SNN baseline.

Small object detection in aerial imagery is crucial for the intelligent interpretation of remote sensing images. However, features of small objects, such as texture and boundaries, are often obscured by complex backgrounds, making effective feature extraction difficult. Traditional methods typically enhance small object features by incorporating shallow feature layers, leading to higher computational costs and post-processing complexity. To address these issues, we propose a Multi-scale Edge-enhanced and Feature-fused Detector (MEF-DETR), which integrates three key innovations to enhance small object detection performance. Firstly, we design MEHANet, a lightweight backbone that explicitly reinforces structural boundary priors across multiple resolutions to mitigate indistinct feature representation. Secondly, we introduce the Channel-wise Cross Fusion Transformer, which facilitates cross-scale semantic calibration by utilizing channel-aware attention to recalibrate discriminative features and suppress background-dominated noise. Finally, we propose the Cross-Stage Omni-LD Feature Pyramid Network, an efficiency-aware neck that enables multi-domain knowledge mining through linear parameter-efficient convolutions and frequency-spatial domain complementarity. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets—VisDrone 2019, RSOD, and UAVVaste—demonstrate that MEF-DETR achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to competitors, achieving a 3.1% improvement in AP and a 4.8% increase in AP50 on the VisDrone dataset. Similar gains are observed on the other datasets, and visualization results further confirm the robustness and accuracy of our model in diverse environments.

Salient Object Detection in Optical Remote Sensing Images (ORSI-SOD) is vital for applications such as urban planning and disaster monitoring. Yet, existing Artificial Neural Network (ANN) models remain energy-intensive and unsuitable for edge deployment. Based on this, we propose a Low-ENergy Spiking Neural Network (LENS-Net) for remote sensing saliency, the first fully spiking neural network for ORSI-SOD. LENS-Net employs an improved Spike-Driven Transformer v3 (SDTv3) encoder to extract multi-scale features with low-energy cost, and a novel Spike Multi-scale Attention Decoder (SpikeMAD) that fuses contextual cues via spike-driven channel attention and up-convolution, ensuring effective saliency representation under sparse computation. Moreover, to stabilize training and improve boundary recognition in complex scenes, we propose a Soft-Clip Spike Firing Approximation (SC-SFA). Across three benchmark datasets, LENS-Net demonstrates outstanding performance while maintaining high energy efficiency, outperforming all lightweight ANN counterparts. For instance, on the ORSSD dataset under a timestep T=4 during inference, LENS-Net achieves a Sα of 92.79%, an MAE of 0.0109, and consumes only 11.48 mJ of energy. These results establish an efficient, low-energy solution for practical ORSI-SOD deployment. The source code is available at: https://github.com/7dra/LENS-Net.

Molecular generation is a core task in computer-aided drug design and is particularly important for structure-based drug design (SBDD). However, effectively capturing complex spatial conformations and maintaining geometric equivariance during the molecular generation process remains a major challenge. Therefore, we propose a diffusion-based generative model called QEGT-Diff, a framework for molecular generation based on a quaternion-equivariant graph Transformer. We first employ a position-modulated Kolmogorov–Arnold network, which utilizes learnable B-spline functions on edges to achieve superior geometric awareness compared to standard MLPs and GNNs. Next, quaternion-equivariant graph layers explicitly incorporates quaternion into the message-passing mechanism, enabling direct modeling of local rotational information and enhancing geometric equivariance. A Transformer module is then applied to capture long-range dependencies, allowing the model to integrate global chemical context. By combining local geometric modeling with global context aggregation, QEGT-Diff enables the generation of high-quality 3D molecular structures. Furthermore, we designed an affinity-entropy loss function to jointly optimize for binding affinity and chemical validity during training. Experiments on the CrossDocked2020 benchmark demonstrate that QEGT-Diff achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of structural accuracy, chemical validity, and molecular diversity.

Sequence-based protein binding site prediction is critical for drug design and biomolecular analysis, enabling the identification of binding residues even when protein structures are unknown. Although sequence-based approaches have advanced, accurately predicting binding sites from one-dimensional sequences remains challenging, limiting both prediction accuracy and robustness. Here, we present MC-GNNPsite, a novel sequence-based method that leverages structures predicted by ESMFold. The model integrates diverse residue features, including physicochemical and evolutionary information, and constructs multi-scale protein graphs using four distance thresholds to capture spatial interactions. A multi-channel graph neural network with an attention mechanism adaptively fuses these multi-scale features for binding site classification. Extensive evaluation on independent datasets demonstrates that MC-GNNPsite outperforms existing sequence-based methods by 8–15% on key metrics, offering not only higher accuracy but also practical utility for offline and batched computational screening when feature generation is precomputed.

AI-assisted materials design increasingly leverages large language models (LLMs) to automate complex research workflows. However, existing systems still lack a structured mechanism for task decomposition and dependency-aware multi-step execution, making it difficult to reliably coordinate heterogeneous knowledge and domain tools in complex materials design tasks. We propose KnowMat, an LLM-based materials agent that integrates specialized knowledge and enables tool learning via a dependency-aware dynamic planning strategy. KnowMat builds a unified knowledge foundation that aligns heterogeneous data sources into a schema-based representation for cross-stage reasoning. On top of this grounding, it explicitly models inter-task constraints to support reliable task planning. The task dependencies guide tool selection and invocation, as well as final response generation based on verified intermediate results. We evaluate KnowMat on a benchmark of superalloy design tasks spanning information retrieval, material screening, and property prediction. KnowMat achieves 92.5% task-decomposition F1, 88.5% workflow execution success, and 84.5% goal completion, outperforming chain-of-thought and static planning baselines. An additional case study on inorganic ABX3 perovskites further verifies that the framework can be adapted to a different materials domain with distinct knowledge bases, task targets, and toolchains. Results further show robust scalability with an increasing number of noisy tools, indicating that dependency modeling is effective for reliable materials design automation.

Recent research on anomaly detection in power grid communications has evolved from traditional rule-based systems to deep learning paradigms. However, the complex spatio-temporal dependencies of network traffic and the lack of labeled samples limit the practical performance of existing models. To address this, we propose an unsupervised Spatio-Temporal Graph Autoencoder framework. By modeling network traffic as dynamic directed graphs, this framework integrates Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units to jointly encode spatial correlations and temporal dynamics into a low-dimensional latent space. Our method characterizes normal traffic patterns using only benign samples and identifies anomalies by measuring the reconstruction error between the observed traffic and the learned normal profile. We perform evaluations on the UNSW-NB15 benchmark and a real-world power grid network dataset. Our method not only achieves high detection accuracies of 95.20% and 94.28% on the respective datasets, but also delivers superior comprehensive performance on the UNSW-NB15 benchmark with an F1-score of 95.22%, a precision of 94.80%, and a recall of 95.65%. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method outperforms supervised baselines and standalone deep learning models, effectively improving the accuracy and robustness of anomaly detection for power grid communication networks.

Zero-shot anomaly detection (ZSAD) aims to identify defects of unseen categories without using task-specific training data. A key challenge in this field is to seamlessly fuse heterogeneous vision foundation models while ensuring fine-grained adaptation to diverse anomaly scenarios. To address this challenge, we propose DLR (Decouple, Localize, Route), a unified framework that addresses modality incompatibility, anomaly diversity and spatial inhomogeneity via feature disentanglement and patch-level adaptive routing strategies. Specifically, the DMFD module resolves the feature heterogeneity of CLIP, DINOv2 and SAM by disentangling their extracted features into independent feature subspaces, and reconciles distinct feature domains by leveraging residual projection and subspace alignment mechanisms. The PGAL component constructs a hierarchical mask pyramid for multi-scale anomaly localization, which enables the accurate capture of spatial variations across different defect types. In addition, the ATSR module fuses multi-metric confidence scores to dynamically assign each image patch to the most reliable subspace, thus matching the unique characteristics of the detected anomaly. With the backbones (CLIP, DINOv2, SAM) frozen and lightweight task heads adopted (4.12M parameters, 180 ms inference latency), DLR achieves state-of-the-art performance: it attains 95.6% Image-AUROC and 93.5% Pixel-AUROC on the MVTec-AD dataset, and 85.5% Image-AUROC and 96.2% Pixel-AUROC on the VisA dataset. DLR also exhibits excellent performance on real industrial fabric defect data collected from actual production lines, and its performance is significantly superior to that of existing advanced methods. Extensive ablation experiments verify the complementary effects of each module in DLR, and the framework maintains high computational efficiency simultaneously.

Accurate prediction of protein essentiality is crucial for understanding organism survival, advancing drug discovery, and informing disease treatment strategies. While traditional computational methods for protein essentiality prediction have relied on network-based approaches, recent advancements have increasingly shifted focus to sequence-based methods. However, existing sequence-based methods often restrict their scope to only sequence-level features, overlooking valuable biological information at other levels. Therefore, in this study, we propose EssLM-MoE, a novel Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)-enhanced framework that integrates diverse levels of biological information to enhance the performance of protein essentiality prediction. EssLM-MoE leverages three pre-trained protein language models, i.e., ProtTrans, ESMFold and OntoProtein, which enables collectively encode multi-level biological information, including sequence, conservation, structure, and function-level biological information. These representations are first refined using convolutional neural networks, and were followed by a MoE-enhanced Transformer module is to capture global dependencies and modality-specific heterogeneity. This enables adaptive and context-aware interaction modeling across sequence-, structure-, and function-aware representations. Experimental results demonstrate that EssLM-MoE consistently outperforms existing computational methods. Ablation studies and case studies further validate the effectiveness of combining diverse protein language models and the MoE architecture. Enrichment analysis reveals that EssLM-MoE successfully identifies essential proteins associated with critical biological functions. In summary, all results highlight the potential of EssLM-MoE in protein essentiality prediction. The source code can be obtained from https://github.com/CSUBioGroup/EssLM-MoE.

Precise drug-drug interaction prediction (DDIP) is fundamental to pharmaceutical innovation and clinical decision support because it helps reveal potentially beneficial and adverse pharmacological interactions between drugs. Graph-based formulations of DDIs provide a natural foundation for this task, and hypergraph representations are especially attractive because they can model higher-order relations that are difficult to express with ordinary pairwise graphs. Nevertheless, existing hypergraph convolutional neural networks (HGCNs) still face two important limitations: coarse molecular representations may overlook fine-grained structural patterns, and static hypergraph construction may fail to adapt to the most informative relational structure during training. To address these issues, we propose a Dynamic Dual Hypergraph Convolutional Neural Network (DDHCNN) for fine-grained DDI prediction. The proposed architecture combines dual-drug representations built from Morgan fingerprints, an attention-based hypergraph learning framework, and a dynamic hyperedge adjustment mechanism that refines the hypergraph structure during training.

Online early fault detection (EFD) is a key step in predictive maintenance, focusing on reliable alarm of fault occurrence in non-stop scenarios. However, online EFD in real-world engineering faces two major challenges: (1) distribution drift in online data, which causes decision bias, and (2) frequent false alarms triggered by traditional hard-boundary (e.g., a single hypersphere enclosing normal instances) decisions in noisy environments. To address these concerns, this paper proposes a novel probabilistic risk-aware anomaly detection method using transfer learning. First, a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) establishes a latent space using normal state data, where a hypersphere annulus-formed one-class detection rule defines three fine-grained states: normal, suspected, and anomalous. Next, a new probabilistic rule adaptation mechanism with domain-adversarial training transfers discriminative knowledge from offline machines to optimize target machine’s detection boundary, improving the identification of both real anomalies and suspected samples. Finally, a probability-aware alarm strategy maps the boundary distance into a continuous risk probability, effectively characterizing the gradual evolution of faults. Experiments on the MNIST∼USPS object recognition anomaly detection and a real-world bearing dataset collected from a steel factory in China demonstrate that the proposed method effectively suppresses false alarms. It achieves highly accurate and timely alarm triggering for online EFD, offering a robust and practical solution for industrial applications.

Industrial anomaly detection relies on representations that clearly separate normal and anomalous patterns, yet anomalous samples are scarce in practice. Existing approaches either reuse generic pre-trained features that are misaligned with the detection objective, or adapt features on the target data only after scarcity has already constrained learning, so the shortage of anomalous variation is never addressed during representation learning itself. We propose DARL (Diffusion-Augmented Representation Learning), a pre-training framework that confronts anomaly scarcity directly while shaping an anomaly-aware feature space. A defect-aware conditional diffusion model synthesizes diverse anomalies on normal images, supplying structured supervision in place of missing real defects. A disentangled contrastive objective, implemented through an orthogonal subspace attention projector, factorizes the representation into a content component and an anomaly-sensitive component, and pulls the anomaly-sensitive features of normal samples toward the origin, so that a simple feature norm acts as the anomaly score. On five industrial benchmarks (MVTec AD, VisA, BTAD, MVTec 3D-AD, and MPDD), this norm-based score matches or surpasses more complex detectors, and further improves them when used as their feature backbone, while remaining effective under few-shot, low-data, and label-noise conditions. By shaping an anomaly-aware feature space at the pre-training stage, DARL turns anomaly scoring into a simple norm computation without sacrificing accuracy.

The convergence of quantum computing and neuromorphic engineering provides an important context for addressing the energy efficiency bottlenecks of classical deep learning and the noise constraints of Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. Quantum Spiking Neural Networks (QSNNs), which integrate the biological plausibility of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) with the high-dimensional state space of quantum systems, have emerged as a promising paradigm for quantum-neuromorphic learning. However, the field faces significant theoretical and algorithmic challenges, primarily the “encoding mismatch” between discrete spikes and continuous quantum states, and the “double non-differentiability” arising from spiking dynamics and quantum measurements. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of QSNNs from an algorithmic and architectural perspective. First, we establish a conceptual homology linking the integrate-and-fire mechanism of biological neurons to unitary quantum evolution and measurement-induced collapse. Second, we systematically categorize existing quantum neuron models (e.g., measurement-driven, continuous evolution, and variational models). Third, we analyze existing training methodologies, synthesizing the divergent paths of evolutionary search and gradient-based tuning. Based on this literature synthesis, we identify a conceptual “Hybrid Co-Optimization Paradigm” as an important future research direction to mitigate the “barren plateau” problem. Finally, we review benchmarks spanning from classical imaging to emerging 2026 applications in genomics and 5G networks. Our analysis suggests an emerging shift towards hybrid architectures, indicating that bio-mimetic mechanisms (e.g., unmeasured qubit memory) may offer useful computational pathways for complex temporal tasks, although empirical quantum advantage over classical baselines remains an open challenge. We conclude by identifying critical hardware challenges, notably the “readout bottleneck,” to guide future research toward hybrid neuro-quantum co-design.

The aim of few-shot point cloud semantic segmentation is to assign semantic labels to novel classes given a few labeled point clouds. Many recent studies have attempted to obtain multiple prototypes for each semantic class to determine the semantic labels of query data. Nevertheless, due to the scarcity of labeled support data and the high variation among query data, obtaining representative prototypes is challenging. To address these challenges, we propose a prototype-free framework called the Mutually-Guided Dual-Incidence Hypergraph Neural Network (MGDI-HGNN). We exploit geometric correlations and spatial proximities among data in both the support and query sets to construct multiple hypergraphs. We then develop a semi-supervised mutual learning process, allowing the learning process of each hypergraph to be guided by supervision from support points across other constructed hypergraphs. Furthermore, we introduce a dual-incidence hypergraph neural network that decouples hyperedge-centric and hypernode-centric topologies to capture asymmetric connectivity patterns between hypernodes and hyperedges. Building upon this dual-incidence structure, we develop a novel inverse-free spatial hypergraph convolution that efficiently updates hypernode representations through decoupled and direction-aware information propagation. A semantic label prediction mechanism based on the most similar support points is then adopted to obtain query predictions within each hypergraph. Finally, semantic labels are assigned to query data by aggregating predictions across all hypergraphs. Extensive evaluations on the S3DIS and ScanNet benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed MGDI-HGNN outperforms state-of-the-art methods in all experimental settings.

Autonomous on-ramp merging is a safety-critical and highly interactive driving task that requires reliable feasibility, safety assurance, and timely maneuver completion. However, existing reinforcement learning (RL) approaches often suffer from low sample efficiency in such high-dimensional and highly dynamic environments, and pure reward-driven exploration struggles to accommodate driving safety and efficiency objectives, leading to either overly aggressive or overly conservative driving behaviors. To address this challenge, we propose PR-EPK, a physics-informed residual RL framework that integrates model-based and analytical expert knowledge into both policy learning and execution. An MPC-based prior provides dynamically feasible baseline controls, while the RL agent learns bounded residual corrections to refine expert behavior, improving exploration efficiency and convergence stability. A risk-adaptive hybrid execution mechanism further regulates residual authority online as a soft safety heuristic during execution. In addition, a decoupled dual-critic constrained learning scheme separates task-return and safety-cost estimation to mitigate objective coupling, and a progressive curriculum strategy gradually transitions from expert-guided training to autonomous policy enhancement. Simulation results across varying traffic densities demonstrate that PR-EPK achieves faster and more stable convergence, consistently higher success rates, significantly reduced collision rates and shorter average merge times compared with representative baselines. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework and demonstrate that structured integration of expert knowledge within residual RL provides a practical pathway toward safe and efficient autonomous merging in highly dynamic traffic.

This paper studies the event-triggered reinforcement learning control for a flexible manipulator system with asymmetric dynamic output multi-constraints. The distributed parameter model of the system is established based on the Hamiltonian principle, which can avoid the problem of control spillover. An actor-critic structure reinforcement learning controller is designed by using a neural network to approximate the system cost function and model uncertainties, while ensuring the optimal performance of the system. A time-varying asymmetric barrier Lyapunov function is considered to ensure the output multi-constraints of the system regarding angle errors and vibrations. The event-triggering mechanism is introduced to dynamically adjust the triggering conditions, avoiding Zeno behavior and reducing communication frequency resources. The proposed controller can not only complete time-varying trajectory tracking, but also guarantee the vibration suppression of the flexible manipulator. The stability of the closed-loop system is proved via Lyapunov’ s direct method. Finally, the effectiveness of the control strategy is verified through numerical simulations and experiments by using the Quanser experimental platform.

The numerical solution of parametric partial differential equations (PDEs) often demands significant computational resources, especially when evaluations must be repeated across a wide parameter space. Neural operator frameworks such as DeepONet offer a viable solution through learning mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces. However, their general-purpose design is not always well-suited for solving PDEs within a restricted but well-defined family of problems. To overcome this challenge, we present HBPP, a Transformer-inspired physics-informed architecture that adapts operator learning into a specialized, problem-aware solver. Unlike standard architectures, which suffer from issues such as the spectral bias of MLPs and rigid mechanisms for coupling function representations with spatial queries, HBPP reinterprets operator learning through attention-based interactions. Building on the DeepONet framework, HBPP replaces its basic dot-product structure with a richer, transformer-like formulation: a branch component processes the input function to produce key vectors, while a trunk network encodes query coordinates into a query. A third transformation network generates dynamic value vectors conditioned jointly on the input function and query location. Additionally, a scaling sub-network normalizes query coordinates based on global properties of the input, improving both training stability and expressive power. We introduce and analyze two variants of the HBPP framework. The first employs a diverse but fixed set of basis functions (e.g., Gaussian random fields, Fourier modes, wavelets) to approximate the input function space, showing strong performance on challenging PDEs such as the KdV–Burgers equation. The second variant abandons fixed bases in favor of learnable basis functions, realized as small neural networks that adapt to the underlying problem structure. Applied to Burgers’ equation and the damped harmonic oscillator, this approach discovers efficient, problem-specific representations. Both versions are trained end-to-end using a physics-informed loss that requires only boundary and initial conditions, avoiding reliance on precomputed solution data. We further present HBPP-Op, a minimal architectural extension that restores a standard operator interface, enabling generalization to unseen input functions; theoretical analysis establishes universal approximation, consistency, and a posteriori error bounds for the framework. All the codes are available at https://github.com/SafariMahdi/HBPP.

This paper proposes a dual-subsystem cooperative control architecture for a class of affine nonlinear systems. By employing a cooperative weighting function that satisfies the convex combination mechanism, the architecture achieves deep integration of reinforcement learning-based port-Hamiltonian (RL-PH) control and RL-based sliding mode control (RL-SMC). Specifically, the first subsystem aims to enhance steady-state performance. By parameterizing damping injection and additional energy, a reinforcement learning algorithm is adopted to online tune the unknown parameters. This approach not only avoids the complexity of solving the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman partial differential equation within the PH framework, but also realizes optimal PH control. The second subsystem focuses on improving transient performance. By constructing a cost function associated with the sliding surface, the conventional SMC is transformed into an optimal control problem, which is approximated by a critic neural network (NN). Furthermore, a nested updating law is meticulously designed to strictly guarantee the asymptotic stability of the NN weight estimation error. Finally, a Gaussian function-based cooperative mechanism is constructed to achieve the seamless fusion of the two control laws. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed strategy significantly outperforms the standalone RL-PH or RL-SMC methods in terms of both steady-state accuracy and dynamic response speed.

A central objective in neuroscience is to elucidate how the brain generates complex dynamic activity through the interactions of brain areas. In this study, we utilized the Interaction Network, a graph neural network model, to develop a computational framework for predicting whole-brain cortical blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) signals. We derived an Inter-Regional Interactions (IRI) metric to quantify message transmission among brain areas probing the underlying dynamical mechanisms. In addition, the total IRI emitted from each brain region was calculated and defined as the IRI sent by region (RS-IRI). Our model predicted BOLD activity for the following 10 time points from initial BOLD signals, and achieved a mean absolute error of 0.04 (arbitrary units). The predicted functional connectivity (FC) achieves a correlation coefficient of 0.97 compared to the empirical FC. The fluctuation amplitude of the IRI increases with the length of the connection and the largest RS-IRI oscillation amplitude is observed in visual areas. The RS-IRI demonstrates a hierarchical organization, characterized by more concentrated distributions in association regions and larger fluctuation amplitudes in unimodal regions. Applying our approach to Alzheimer’s disease (AD), we demonstrate that the frequency-specific amplitudes of IRI oscillations discriminate AD patients from healthy controls and correlate with Mini-Mental State Examination scores. Together, this work presents a deep learning–based framework for modeling brain dynamics as well as a quantitative index of inter-areal interactions, and offers a new perspective for disease characterization.

Accurate forecasting of photovoltaic power is critical for the large-scale integration of renewable energy into smart grids. However, the task remains challenging due to the complex periodicity inherent in weather regimes and the intricate interdependence of meteorological variables. To address this, we propose the CVSC-Transformer. The model first employs the Fast Fourier Transform to project multivariate time series into the frequency-domain, then decomposes each complex spectrum into its real and imaginary components. By strategically reorienting the sequence axis as the variable axis, it explicitly learns cross-variable spectral dependency while rigorously preserving amplitude-phase consistency. Learnable frequency weights are further incorporated to adaptively emphasize critical spectral components, and a dual-branch Transformer encoder is employed to capture inter-variable correlations. The final forecast is generated through an inverse transform followed by a linear projection. Extensive experiments on five real-world datasets demonstrate that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance in most scenarios, with particularly pronounced advantages in long-term prediction tasks. This work offers a practical and high-performance solution for PV forecasting, effectively overcoming key limitations of existing methods and contributing to the advancement of renewable energy integration.

Partial differential equations (PDEs) are fundamental tools for modeling complex physical processes in natural and engineered systems. Neural operators have emerged as a powerful framework for learning nonlinear mappings between function spaces, enabling efficient solutions for families of PDEs. However, existing neural operators often rely on large-scale models and energy-intensive training, limiting their practicality in energy-constrained environments. Moreover, they exhibit limited capacity in capturing temporal dependencies inherent in dynamic PDEs. To address these limitations, we propose LDNO, a low-power dynamic neural operator built on the Liquid State Machine (LSM) for time-dependent operator learning. LDNO adopts a dual-branch architecture in which the LSM branch performs event-driven dynamic feature encoding while a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) branch captures long-horizon dependencies. A multi-strategy DownSampling module is introduced to reduce the input dimensionality of the LSM branch, and an adaptive cross-fusion module is designed to dynamically integrate branch outputs for efficient multiscale spatiotemporal representation learning. Experiments on challenging PDE benchmarks show that LDNO delivers competitive overall accuracy and particularly strong results on selected time-dependent PDE benchmarks under the present experimental protocol. Under an operation-level energy model adopted for this study, LDNO is estimated to reduce inference energy Einf by 90.24%–99.81% relative to the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) and by 81.70%–99.81% relative to the Wavelet Neural Operator (WNO) across five PDE benchmarks. Supplementary delay differential equation (DDE) experiments in the appendix further provide auxiliary evidence for the potential extension of LDNO to delay dynamics.

Molecular generation has emerged as a key technology in computer-aided drug design, materials science, and synthetic chemistry, allowing the de novo design of new compounds with specific functional properties for diverse applications. Traditional molecular design methods rely heavily on experimental screening, and rule-based strategies face significant limitations, including prohibitive costs, long cycle time, and limited exploration of chemical space. Through data-driven methods, recent advances in deep learning have greatly accelerated the progress of molecular design, producing a variety of generative models that address these underlying challenges. Recent studies demonstrate remarkable improvements in many areas, from architectural innovations in generative frameworks to enhanced exploration of chemical diversity and targeted molecular optimization. This review systematically summarizes state-of-the-art deep learning methods for molecular generation, benchmark datasets, practical implementation details, quantitative performance comparisons, and evaluation metrics, and further discusses emerging challenges related to LLM-based molecular generation, large-molecule design, scalability, polypharmacology, off-target effects, and ethical considerations.

Dynamic graph anomaly detection is crucial for identifying abnormal interactions in a wide range of real-world systems, such as social media, e-commerce, and cybersecurity. Existing methods commonly encode graph snapshots independently and subsequently aggregate their temporal representations, limiting their ability to preserve temporally relevant long-range evidence while explicitly capturing fine-grained structural evolution across snapshots. Moreover, directly extending the historical observation window may introduce irrelevant information and excessive computational cost. To address these challenges, we propose CHGNN, a Context-Aware Hierarchical Graph Neural Network that jointly captures long- and short-term dependencies for edge-level anomaly detection in dynamic graphs. For long-term modeling, CHGNN employs a temporal-decay graph diffusion strategy that assigns larger sampling budgets to recent snapshots and smaller budgets to distant ones, and then connects the sampled subgraphs through shared target nodes to construct a compact global graph. This design enables efficient cross-temporal information propagation while suppressing less relevant historical information. For short-term modeling, a context-aware hierarchical aggregation mechanism treats adjacent snapshots as contextual environments to encode fine-grained structural transitions, while attention-based propagation on the global graph captures long-term structural evolution. A learnable feature-wise gating module subsequently integrates the complementary short- and long-term representations for anomaly scoring. Experiments on five benchmark datasets against twelve representative baselines under three anomaly ratios show that CHGNN achieves the highest mean AUC across all evaluated settings. Ablation and sensitivity analyses further confirm its effectiveness and robustness.

To address the accurate dynamic modeling and online parameter identification of quadrotor unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) under varying-payload operating conditions, this paper proposes a Data-driven Physical Iterative with Physics-Informed Neural Network (DPI-PINN) hybrid framework. The DPI module constructs a feature library grounded in the Newton-Euler equations of the quadrotor and online estimates dominant physical parameters including rotational inertia and vehicle mass via sliding-window least squares, enabling an interpretable dominant dynamic model that tracks abrupt parameter variations such as payload changes in real time. The PINN module compensates for the residual dynamics by learning a residual acceleration correction under kinematic ordinary differential equation constraints parameterized by the DPI-identified parameters, ensuring that the physics-informed supervision adapts jointly with the online dominant model. Real-flight experiments demonstrate an 11.1% reduction in one-step angular rate root-mean-square error (RMSE) over DPI alone, a mean rotational inertia identification error of 4.1%, and successful mass tracking from 1.710 kg to 2.035 kg under a 2.5 s sliding-window setting.

Stress detection is a major challenge faced today since it is not apparent and also because the human body does not always respond in a predictable manner. To record this stress data, using a single type of sensor, however, can ignore the subtle complexities of the human stress response. In order to address this, a new approach has been suggested in this paper, which treats the body as a single unit by combining brainwaves with heart rate and behavioral data. In order to make the data that they gather reflect the human stress cycle in detail, the participants were subjected to four various scenarios: relaxation, stress, Heartfulness meditation and recovery. This allowed the coordination of various physiological signals into one rappy system capable of perceiving stress as it is known in the real world. The algorithm identifies distinct neural signals amidst the noise produced during normal movements with extensive filter advice and Independent Component Analysis (ICA). It then matches such detailed brainwave patterns with important heart rate and blood pressure information. The system compares these physiological measures with the psychometric PSS-10 scale, thus, creating a multi-layered assessment of stress which is both clinically meaningful and technically correct. The consistency of the system has been tested, with the Leave-One-Subject-Out (LOSO) verification procedure, which indicates the model is widely applicable to the model on previously unknown individuals with varying physiological parameters. The experimental results indicate that the ensemble model achieved an accuracy of 99.33%, which is much higher than the traditional methods based solely on EEG or cardiovascular signals. Furthermore, the system responds in less than two seconds, which means that it is fast enough to be utilized in real-life applications or even medical devices or clinical systems to assist individuals in managing stress as soon as it occurs.

Spatial transcriptomics has emerged as a transformative technology for interrogating tissue microenvironments, enabling high resolution gene expression profiling while preserving precise spatial context. This capability provides novel insights into cellular spatial distribution patterns and the structural functional relationships underlying tissue organization. However, current methods for spatial domain identification face significant limitations, particularly in simultaneously modeling local spatial continuity and global molecular heterogeneity. Furthermore, existing approaches often inadequately integrate high-dimensional gene expression features with complex spatial topologies, leading to suboptimal accuracy in domain delineation. To overcome these challenges, we present a Bidirectional Augmented Spatial Transcriptomics framework (BiAugST). Firstly, we propose a bidirectional expression augmentation strategy tailored to address spatial heterogeneity: positive augmentation employs spatial neighborhood smoothing to reinforce local continuity, while negative augmentation utilizes adversarial perturbations to improve the representation of global heterogeneity. For effective integration of spatial and feature information, we design a dual-channel graph neural network that jointly encodes multi-order topological interactions from the spatial proximity graph and the positive-enhanced feature similarity graph. Additionally, we introduce a reconstruction contrastive joint optimization mechanism that enhances generalization capability through discriminative training using positive and negative sample pairs. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BiAugST effectively addresses the aforementioned issues, achieving competitive performance across multiple benchmark datasets from diverse technological platforms.
